chapter: Opinions on pop music, jazz education and the business
title: Berklee's philosophy and Juilliard dropping jazz
summary: Wilson explains Berklee trains working musicians, and recalls Schuman's Juilliard course, later piano-only under Mehegan, was discontinued.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Well, the Berklee philosophy is to turn out a musician who can make a living in music -- Is that what the objective is? isn't that the overall thing they try to do? A guy who doesn't have to drive a cab or take a job in a department store, if he can be a full time musician? And they try to teach him to read music, to play pop music, to play jazz, to improvise and to sit in a section and play jazz, play some Latin rhythm, the whole business, that can pay a musician a buck to do it.
You said -- in the course of these tapings over these few hours, you said that was what happened at Juilliard, when the man who was in charge of Juilliard was trying to do.
Well, it just so happens that recently someone offered Juilliard a grant for a jazz study, and they refused it.
Yeah. They're out of that now. Yeah. They got away from jazz years ago.
That's what I said -- all that was just a political move at the time; everybody was saying they were interested in the history of jazz and the black music, but that was just politics.
But the young man who took over Juilliard back in 1945, William Shuman, the composer, that was his idea.
But now, William Shuman -- Juilliard is a small part of his interests now; he's head of all of Lincoln Center now.

So maybe who's ever setting up the curriculum at Juilliard now, Shuman doesn't concern himself with it, I don't know. But they dropped it -- well, they never really went all out with jazz. After me, they had Johnny Mehegan up there, but it wasn't broad like Berklee, it was just piano only.

See, Berklee has everything there -- rhythm, jazz, horns, drums, guitars, everything. But in Juilliard, there was never anything except piano. It started with me in summer school for eight years and then they had Johnny Mehegan up there, 15 or 20 years, but just with piano.
